name: Bilal Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a ten-year-old hatchback for three apps: two food ones and a grocery one that pays more per drop but wants you to carry six bags up to flats. Every morning I ask an AI chat which parts of town were busiest the same day last week, and it reads my earnings spreadsheet and tells me where to sit. I usually start at ten near the retail park on the east side and finish around nine. I live with my partner Jess, who's in her second year of nursing, so right now my driving pays most of the rent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The car eats me alive: fuel, tyres, the insurance that jumped last year. I'm still not great at the job, honestly; I miss turnings and I'm slower with the grocery bags than the guys who've done it for years. What I like is the puzzle. I treat it like a game, moving between apps and zones, and some nights I beat my own record by thirty percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I like this stuff. I'd post my spreadsheet trick so other drivers can use the AI bits that do work. And I'd still say the apps should pay a fair base fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I stay a driver longer than I planned, with a car that's getting older. The squeeze from fuel and insurance doesn't care about AI. Jess qualifies in eighteen months, and until then it's mostly on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving three apps and keep using the AI to plan my zones, because it already earns me maybe fifty more a week. I'd put a bit aside each month for a newer car, because the hatchback won't last. I'd go to the drivers' association meeting, because I want a say in the fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Relieved for other people, but I was kind of looking forward to something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the car breaks down in those eighteen months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the nightmare. I've got about three months of rent saved, and a new gearbox would take a third of it. I'd borrow Jess's dad's car for a week and drive every hour I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to the drivers' association. What would you push for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clear fee per kilometre, published, so the app can't change it quietly. I'd also push for drivers to see the data the app collects on us. If my spreadsheet can see patterns, so can the app's, and the app is using those patterns against drivers.

say: I'd say I'm **disappointed**, because I like what the tools can do.
I'd share my **spreadsheet trick** and still call for a fair **base fee**.
think: Privately, I stay a **driver** longer, in an ageing car that costs more each year.
Until Jess **qualifies**, the rent is mostly on me.
do: Keep using AI to **plan zones**, which earns about fifty more a week.
Save monthly for a **newer car** before the hatchback dies.
Push the drivers' association for a **published fee** per kilometre.
feel: A bit **flat**, because he was looking forward to something new.
S0.quote: If my spreadsheet can see patterns, so can the app's, and the app is using those patterns against drivers.
fieldNote: He already uses AI daily to **earn more**, unlike most drivers he knows.
His real pressure is **car costs** and carrying rent while his partner studies.
He wants drivers to see the **data** the apps hold on them.

steps.text: Keep asking an AI chat which zones to work each morning
Put money aside monthly for a newer car
Push the drivers' association for a published per-kilometre fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say drivers who learn the tools will do better, and the apps should share what they save with us. Online I'd post how-to videos. I'd also back a law that says the app must explain its pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this is good for me for a few years, because my job is mostly hands-on and I'm ahead on the thinking bits. The danger is the apps using smarter software to set my pay. I'd want to understand it before it understands me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an online course on fleet and logistics software, the kind depots use to plan routes, maybe two evenings a week. I'd keep driving full time. I'd look at an electric vehicle technician course too, because cars and robots will need fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a bit nervous. Like the start of a new level in a game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to understand it before it understands you. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keeping my own records of every order, time and fee, and checking them against what the app paid. Last month I found the app underpaid me for twelve long trips, so I sent an AI-written complaint and got the money back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Jess make of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jess thinks I'm a bit obsessed. But she also likes that I've got a plan, because she's the one who'll have the steady job. We joke that she'll look after people and I'll look after the robots.

say: I'd say drivers who learn the **tools** do better, and apps should **share savings**.
I'd back a law forcing apps to **explain pay**.
think: My job is mostly **hands-on**, and I'm ahead on the thinking parts.
The real danger is **smarter pay software** setting my income.
do: Take an **online fleet software** course two evenings a week.
Look into an **electric vehicle** technician course.
feel: Mostly **excited**, a bit **nervous**, like starting a new game level.
S1.quote: Last month I found the app underpaid me for twelve long trips, so I sent an AI-written complaint and got the money back.
fieldNote: He treats AI as an **advantage** and already uses it to catch underpayment.
His worry is **pay algorithms**, not robots, in this picture.
His partner's coming **nursing job** gives the household a steady anchor.

steps.text: Check every app payment against his own AI-built records
Take an online fleet software course two evenings a week
Keep driving all three apps full time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules fast: drivers must get a share of what robots save, and paid retraining has to start now. I'd post that the people who built these apps on our backs owe us. I'd join any drivers' campaign going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've got three years at most before robots replace my driving, and the thinking AI will already have made my software course less useful. That's the scary part. My plan was to manage the robots, but by 2028 an AI might manage them better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch straight to the electric vehicle technician course, because fixing the actual machines is hands-on and lasts longer than planning software. I'd cut driving to four days to make time. I'd save harder too, because I'd need a cushion while I'm training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous for real this time. I like change, but this is a lot of change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to save harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, the takeaways I deliver all day and then order myself, and the trip to Jess's cousin's wedding abroad. That's maybe two hundred a month. It'd sting, but it gets me to six months by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be fixing robots that took your job. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weird, honestly. But someone's going to fix them, and I'd rather it was a former driver who knows what they're for. I'd still want the firms taxed properly for it.

say: I'd demand drivers get a **share** of robot savings and **paid retraining** now.
I'd say the app firms **owe** the drivers who built them.
think: Robots replace my driving within **three years** of AGI.
By 2028 AI might **manage robots** better than me, which undoes my plan.
do: Switch straight to the **electric vehicle** technician course.
Cut driving to **four days** a week to make time for training.
Save about **two hundred** more a month by skipping a wedding trip.
feel: **Nervous** for real, because it's a lot of change at once.
S2.quote: My plan was to manage the robots, but by 2028 an AI might manage them better than me.
fieldNote: He quickly **swaps plans** from software to repair once thinking AI arrives first.
The **robot lag** gives him time to retrain for hands-on repair work.
He's uneasy about fixing the machines that **replaced** him but would still do it.

steps.text: Enrol in the electric vehicle technician course right away
Skip the cousin's wedding trip abroad and stop ordering takeaway
Reach six months of savings by 2030
Campaign for drivers to get a share of robot savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the government to plan properly, so drivers should be pushing hard now. I'd keep posting what tools are worth learning. I'd want the drivers' association to negotiate retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is pretty good for me. I'd have time to finish the technician course and get a year or two on the job before robots come for driving in 2034. I'd be thirty-five and already in something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the technician course in the first year, part-time, and keep driving five days. By year three I'd want an apprenticeship at a garage that services electric vans. I'd keep my savings steady rather than cutting hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit uneasy, but it feels like a plan rather than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock the plan off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If every driver in the city has the same idea, the garage places will fill up before I get one. Or there's the chance Jess's placement moves her to another town. I'd go with her, and I'd have to start over with the garages there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, without thinking. Her job's the steadier one, and a nurse can get work anywhere. I can drive or fix cars anywhere too.

I'd want the drivers' association to win **retraining money**.
think: Five years lets me finish the **technician course** before robots arrive.
I'd be **thirty-five** and already in another trade by 2034.

Apply for a **garage apprenticeship** with electric vans by year three.
Keep savings **steady** rather than cutting hard.
feel: **Steady**, a bit **uneasy**, but it feels like a plan.
S3.quote: If every driver in the city has the same idea, the garage places will fill up before I get one.
fieldNote: The extra time turns his worry into a **clear plan** with dates.
His main risk is **competition** for garage places from other drivers.

steps.text: Start the electric vehicle technician course part-time this year
Apply for a garage apprenticeship servicing electric vans by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and the government should make sure every driver gets a funded course. Online I'd say don't wait. I'd keep backing the drivers' association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is plenty for me. I'd have finished with driving long before robots take the vans in 2039. Jess will be a nurse with a few years behind her by then, so the house is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the technician course in the next couple of years, then move into a garage full time. I'd maybe buy a cheap electric car once I know how to fix it myself. I'd keep a little side work doing deliveries at weekends while it still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Even a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a driver who isn't planning anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pick one thing you can do with your hands that a robot will be bad at for a while, and start a course this year. I'd show them my spreadsheet and say it's not magic, just paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the garage jobs pay as well as I hope. If they pay less than driving, I'd be fine with Jess's wage, but I'd feel like I'd gone backwards.

say: I'd call a decade a **gift** and push for a **funded course** for every driver.
I'd tell other drivers **not to wait**.
think: Ten years is **plenty** to leave driving before robots take the vans.
Jess will be an **established nurse**, so the household is steady.
do: Take the **technician course** within the next couple of years.
Buy a cheap **electric car** once he can fix it himself.
Keep **weekend deliveries** going while they still pay.
S4.quote: Pick one thing you can do with your hands that a robot will be bad at for a while, and start a course this year.
fieldNote: With ten years, he sees **driving** as a short chapter rather than his career.
His partner's **steady job** removes most of the household risk.
His only doubt is whether **garage pay** matches driving.

steps.text: Take the electric vehicle technician course within two years
Buy a cheap electric car to practise repairs on
Keep weekend app deliveries going while they still pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my plan to work with the software gets wiped out before I can use it. What would help is paid technician training starting now, and rules so drivers get a share of what the robots save. Nobody's going to hand drivers a share of the savings unless a law makes them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the data. The apps know more about my working day than I do, and they use that knowledge to pay me less. Before any robots show up, I'd want drivers to see their own data.

headlineQuote: The apps know more about my working day than I do, and they use that knowledge to pay me less.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old** car delivery driver working three food and grocery apps.
He uses **AI daily** to pick zones and catch underpayment, and enjoys it like a game.
He pays most of the **rent** while his partner Jess trains as a nurse.
He backs **regulation** and a drivers' share of automation savings.
He moves from **uneasy** to anxious in the fast AGI picture, and is calm with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because thinking AI would wipe out his software plan before it pays off.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **technician training** now, plus rules giving drivers a **share** of robot savings.
Letting drivers see their **own data** from the apps.
